title: JEZEBEL PAINTED HER EYES, FIXED HER HAIR, AND WAITED AT THE WINDOW
paragraphs: JEZEBEL PAINTED HER EYES, FIXED HER HAIR, AND WAITED AT THE WINDOW

She knew judgment was coming. Yet instead of humbling herself before God, she prepared her appearance. The terrifying question is not what Jezebel did at that window—but how many of us are still decorating what Jesus is calling us to surrender.
There is something haunting about a woman fixing her appearance while judgment is approaching the city.
Not because fixing your hair is evil.
And not because Scripture gives us permission to turn every woman wearing cosmetics into some modern caricature of “Jezebel.”
The horror of 2 Kings 9:30 is much deeper than cosmetics.
That is where the verse becomes frightening.
The dynasty around which she had built her power was collapsing.
And the judgment God had spoken years earlier through Elijah was moving toward its fulfillment.
Then Scripture gives us this unforgettable picture:
“Now when Jehu arrived in Jezreel, Jezebel heard of it. So she painted her eyes, adorned her head, and looked down from a window.”
The Hebrew is even more visually striking:
וַתָּשֶׂם בַּפּוּךְ עֵינֶיהָ וַתֵּיטֶב אֶת־רֹאשָׁהּ וַתַּשְׁקֵף בְּעַד הַחַלּוֹן
Vattasem bappukh eineha, vatteitev et-roshah, vattashqef be'ad hachallon.
Literally, the language describes Jezebel putting her eyes “in” or “with” paint, beautifying or adorning her head, and looking down through the window.
Because Scripture does not explicitly tell us exactly what was going through Jezebel's mind.

Some interpreters have understood her appearance as an attempt at seduction or manipulation. Others have seen the actions as royal defiance—a queen determined to face death looking like a queen. The biblical writer does not settle that question for us.
So we shouldn't pretend he does.
But Scripture makes something else unmistakably clear.
And still there is no recorded repentance.
No acknowledgment of the LORD she had opposed.
and prepared herself to meet Jehu.
Because sometimes the most dangerous spiritual condition isn't ignorance.
You can know the sermon was for you and still scroll to the next video.
You can feel conviction during worship and still return to the same secret sin.
You can know you need to apologize and still protect your pride.
You can know the relationship is pulling you away from Christ and still call it love.
You can know bitterness is poisoning your heart and still rehearse what they did to you every night.
You can know your private life is contradicting your public Christianity and still learn how to look spiritual enough that nobody notices.
And still stand at the window as though everything is under control.
That is what makes this story more than ancient history.
There is a little window in every human heart where image and truth eventually meet.
And some of us have become frighteningly good at standing there.
The worship song plays in the car.
“God is good” rolls easily from the mouth.
You're performing Christianity while privately starving for Christ.
That isn't written to crush you.
It is written because being exposed by Christ can become the beginning of being healed by Christ.
Jezebel's story did not begin at the window.

Long before 2 Kings 9, Scripture introduces her as the Sidonian princess who became the wife of Ahab. First Kings 16 says Ahab served Baal and worshiped him. Jezebel became deeply associated with the promotion of Baal worship in Israel. First Kings 18 tells us that prophets of the LORD were being killed and that Jezebel supported hundreds of prophets of Baal and Asherah.
And this is where the story becomes painfully human.
Naboth owned a vineyard beside Ahab's palace.
Naboth refused because the land was his ancestral inheritance.
Letters were written in Ahab's name.
The man who wouldn't sell it to you is dead.
A man dies because powerful people wanted what belonged to him.
And the palace gets its vineyard.
Judgment was pronounced against Ahab's house, and concerning Jezebel came the dreadful prophecy that dogs would devour her in Jezreel.
Because delayed judgment can deceive a rebellious heart into believing judgment has disappeared.
You sinned and woke up the next morning.
So slowly, dangerously, mercy begins to feel like permission.
But Scripture says God's patience has a purpose.
Romans 2:4 asks whether we presume upon the riches of His kindness, not realizing that God's kindness is meant to lead us to repentance.
Mercy is not God's approval of your rebellion.
Mercy is God giving the rebel time to come home.
And that changes how we should read Jezebel at the window.
The tragedy is not merely that judgment finally arrived.
The tragedy is all the opportunities to turn before it did.
How many warnings had passed through her world?
How many demonstrations of God's power?
How many moments in which pride could have broken?
How many opportunities to recognize that Baal was not God?
Yet when the final scene arrives, Scripture records no repentance.
Just a woman at a window.
There are moments when the Bible stops feeling like something you are reading...
Maybe this is one of them.
What are you decorating that Jesus is asking you to surrender?
What are you managing instead of confessing?
What are you explaining instead of repenting of?
What are you keeping alive because admitting the truth would cost you your image?
Maybe they're the carefully edited version of your life everyone else gets to see.
Anything can become camouflage when the heart learns to hide behind it.
And Jesus has never been interested merely in improving camouflage.
He came to resurrect dead people.
That is where Jezebel's window eventually points us beyond Jezebel.
Because if this article ended with Jezebel's death, we could walk away saying, “What a terrible woman.”
The Bible will not allow that.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
The person reading Scripture every morning needs mercy.
The person who hasn't opened a Bible in twenty years needs mercy.
And there is only one Savior.
This is where the window at Jezreel eventually gives way to a hill outside Jerusalem.
Because the Gospel does not announce that good people managed to make themselves presentable enough for God.
The Gospel announces that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Jesus did not wait for you to fix yourself.
And then He carried a cross.
At Calvary, Jesus wasn't covering sin with religious cosmetics.
Isaiah had spoken centuries earlier of the Servant who would be pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities.
At the cross, the holy Son of God bore sin's judgment.
Christ calling sinners to repent and believe.
And that means your story does not have to end at the window.
Your story does not have to end at the window.
You may have slept with someone you shouldn't have.
You may have watched things you would be terrified for your family to discover.
You may have walked away from God.
You may have used religion to hide a heart far from Jesus.
You may have built such a convincing exterior that everyone thinks you're fine.
But while there is breath in your lungs, the call of the Gospel is not:
Stop painting over what needs forgiveness.
Stop defending what Jesus died to deliver you from.
Stop hiding wounds He already sees.
Repentance does not mean making yourself worthy enough for Jesus.
Repentance means turning from sin toward the Savior who is worthy.
The thing you keep deleting from your browser history.
The resentment you've justified for eleven years.
Because grace is not God pretending your sin doesn't matter.
The cross proves that sin matters terribly.
Grace is God doing in Christ what you could never do for yourself.
And this is why “From Scandal to Grace” is more than a phrase.
It is the heartbeat of redemption.
Peter denied Jesus and became a preacher of the risen Christ.
Paul persecuted Christians and became an apostle proclaiming the faith he once tried to destroy.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation, yet he turned toward Christ and heard words of paradise.
Again and again Scripture shows us that God is capable of entering ruined stories.
Grace takes guilty people and, through Christ, makes forgiveness possible.
Not by pretending the first chapters never happened...
but by refusing to let sin have the final word over everyone who comes to Him.
So I want to ask you something more personal than whether you enjoyed this article.
What is happening behind your window?
Not the celebrity whose scandal everybody is discussing.
What would happen if Jesus stripped away every filter tonight?
Would He find someone fighting sin...
or someone learning to live comfortably beside it?
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Your comment may become the sentence another struggling believer reads at 2:13 in the morning and realizes, “I'm not the only one fighting.”
And please don't keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing earns favor with God. It doesn't.
But if you genuinely want your digital life to glorify God, one practical way to do that is to help put biblical truth in front of people who may never walk through a church door.
Even send it privately to the person you know would never respond publicly.
There may come a night when the person who needs to read it again is you.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well.
Supporting Gospel ministry does not replace supporting your local church, caring for your family, giving to people in need, or obeying however God directs your stewardship.
But it can be a practical way of standing behind work you believe is helping proclaim Christ.
Someone may be fixing the outside while their soul is begging for rescue.
Someone may believe they've sinned too badly to come home.
Someone may need to discover tonight that Christianity isn't the story of sinners successfully hiding their stains.
It is the story of a Savior whose blood washes sinners clean.
Jezebel heard judgment approaching and stood at her window.
And right now, through the Gospel, mercy is still calling.
Don't paint over what Jesus is asking you to bring into the light.
Don't decorate the prison when Christ is offering freedom.
Don't spend another year protecting an image while your soul starves behind it.
The window does not have to be the final scene.
Because the most beautiful thing about grace is that Jesus can meet you in the chapter you are ashamed of—and make sure it isn't the chapter that gets the last word.
